factors.name: Opioid painkillers & methadone
factors.headline: Regular opioid use, including methadone, lowers testosterone by about 165 ng/dL in men, and reviews report lower semen quality and higher sperm DNA fragmentation; direct human semen studies are few and low quality.

dose.effective: Effects described with regular (daily) use of any opioid, including maintenance methadone.
dose.studied_range: Cross-sectional and cohort studies of chronic users; no dose-response trials.
dose.too_much: Higher doses and long-acting opioids appear worse; tramadol and tapentadol may cause less suppression.
dose.timeframe: Hormonal suppression develops with regular use; semen recovery after tapering is expected over months but is poorly studied.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Never stop opioids or methadone abruptly; tapering or switching must be supervised. Men on opioids with low testosterone who want children should not be treated with testosterone, which further suppresses sperm production.

factors.mechanism: Opioids suppress hypothalamic GnRH and hence LH and testosterone, increase aromatase, and act on opioid receptors in the testis and on sperm themselves [med-drobnis2017, med-bawor2015].
factors.interactions: Testosterone replacement ([testosterone-anabolic-steroids]) for opioid-induced low testosterone suppresses spermatogenesis; [glp1-agonists] raised testosterone without suppressing LH/FSH in obese men, though not studied in opioid users. [cannabis] is covered separately.
factors.caveats: Opioid users differ from controls in smoking, illness and other drug use, so semen findings are heavily confounded.
factors.debate: The testosterone effect is consistent across 17 studies, though heterogeneous and low quality [med-bawor2015]; the semen and DNA-fragmentation effects rest mainly on narrative review of small studies [med-drobnis2017]. No published study was found arguing opioids are harmless to sperm; the debate is about magnitude and reversibility.

key_numbers.label: Testosterone difference, opioid users vs controls

factors.name: Sulfasalazine & methotrexate (bowel and arthritis drugs)
factors.headline: Sulfasalazine (2-4 g/day) reliably but reversibly damages sperm, with pregnancies typically about 2.5 months after switching; low-dose methotrexate showed no change in semen or sperm DNA fragmentation and no excess birth defects in 127 children of exposed fathers.

dose.effective: Sulfasalazine 2-4 g/day; low-dose weekly methotrexate as used in arthritis, psoriasis and IBD.
dose.studied_range: Sulfasalazine 2-4 g/day for >2 months; methotrexate in 20 men followed prospectively and 127 Danish births.
dose.too_much: Sulfasalazine at any therapeutic dose for over 2 months; high-dose methotrexate as chemotherapy is a different exposure (see chemo-radiation).
dose.timeframe: Sulfasalazine effects reverse within about 2-3 months of switching; methotrexate data cover the 90 days before conception.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Men on sulfasalazine who are trying to conceive can ask about switching to mesalazine or another agent; the ACR guideline supports continuing low-dose methotrexate in men planning conception.

factors.mechanism: The sulphapyridine part of sulfasalazine is toxic to maturing sperm late in their development (rat data show the same effect with sulphapyridine but not 5-aminosalicylic acid) [med-omorain1984]. Methotrexate barely accumulates in sperm because of low folylpolyglutamate synthetase activity [med-perezgarcia2023].
factors.interactions: Underlying inflammatory disease ([chronic-inflammation]) can itself affect fertility; high-dose cytotoxic treatment belongs under [chemo-radiation]. Folate status ([folate-zinc]) is relevant for methotrexate users.
factors.caveats: Sulfasalazine data are older and small but consistent. Methotrexate data come from 20 men and registry births; high-dose regimens are not covered.
factors.debate: Older advice to stop methotrexate 3 months before conception is contested by a Danish registry (aOR 1.01 for malformations) [med-eck2017] and a prospective semen study [med-perezgarcia2023]; reviews still describe its sperm effect as uncertain and note animal testicular toxicity [med-perezgarcia2020, med-banerjee2019]. For sulfasalazine there is no real disagreement: men on it have lower counts and motility than men on mesalazine [med-banerjee2019, med-toovey1981].

factors.name: Alpha-blockers (tamsulosin, silodosin) and ejaculation
factors.headline: Tamsulosin 0.8 mg/day cut ejaculate volume by 2.4 mL and caused complete anejaculation in 35% of healthy men, and 95% of sexually active silodosin users reported ejaculatory disorder; alfuzosin had no such effect.

dose.effective: Tamsulosin 0.4-0.8 mg/day; silodosin 8 mg/day (typical prostate doses).
dose.studied_range: Tamsulosin 0.8 mg/day vs alfuzosin vs placebo (healthy volunteers); silodosin in 91 men with BPH.
dose.too_much: Higher tamsulosin doses and silodosin have the strongest effect.
dose.timeframe: Immediate and reversible on stopping.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Men trying to conceive who take these drugs can ask about an alternative (alfuzosin did not affect ejaculation in the healthy-volunteer trial) or timing.

factors.mechanism: Alpha-1A blockade relaxes the vas deferens, seminal vesicles and bladder neck, reducing emission of semen; the tamsulosin trial found this was not explained by retrograde ejaculation [med-hellstrom2006]. This is a mechanical, not a redox, effect.
factors.interactions: Often combined with [finasteride-sperm] (5-ARIs) for prostate enlargement, which also lowers semen volume.
factors.caveats: Ejaculate volume and anejaculation matter for natural conception; sperm production itself is not shown to be harmed.
factors.debate: No substantive published debate found on the effect itself; the size differs by drug, with tamsulosin and silodosin affecting most men and alfuzosin none in a head-to-head trial [med-hellstrom2006, med-sakata2012].

factors.name: Advanced sperm selection for ICSI (PICSI/hyaluronan, MACS, microfluidics, IMSI)
factors.headline: Selecting 'better' sperm lowers measured DNA fragmentation in the dish but has not raised live birth: PICSI in 2772 couples gave 27.4% vs 25.2% (NS), MACS and microfluidics trials are small and conflicting; HFEA rates PICSI black and SDF-guided selection grey.

dose.effective: Not routinely recommended (ESHRE); microfluidics 'can be considered'. If SDF is high, cheaper first steps are short abstinence and fixing causes.
dose.studied_range: Hyaluronan binding (PICSI), annexin-V magnetic beads (MACS), microfluidic chips, high-magnification morphology (IMSI).
dose.too_much: Extra cost per cycle; no safety signal.
dose.timeframe: Lab step on the day of ICSI.
dose.notes: Cochrane 2026: hyaluronan selection probably slightly reduces miscarriage (RR 0.59, moderate certainty), a secondary outcome.

factors.mechanism: Mature sperm with intact chromatin bind hyaluronan; apoptotic sperm expose phosphatidylserine (removed by MACS); microfluidic channels select motile sperm without the ROS burst of centrifugation. All aim to deliver sperm with less oxidative DNA damage to the egg.
factors.interactions: Alternatives for high SDF: [short-abstinence], [varicocele] repair, [testicular-sperm-icsi]; the egg's repair capacity falls with [maternal-age], so effects might differ by female age.
factors.caveats: Lower DFI in the prepared sample does not translate into live births in trials so far.
factors.debate: A small single-centre RCT reported higher live birth with a microfluidic chip (46.8% vs 25%) [fer-aydin2022], but a 2026 RCT found lower DFI without better live birth [fer-huong2026]; MACS RCTs were null [fer-romany2014, fer-mantravadi2024]. HABSelect was null for live birth [fer-miller2019], while Cochrane 2026 finds a probable miscarriage reduction with hyaluronan selection [fer-garg2026]. ESHRE: not routine, microfluidics 'can be considered' [fer-eshre2023addons]; HFEA: PICSI black, SDF-guided selection grey [fer-hfea2026, fer-hfea2026sdf].

key_numbers.label: Term live birth, PICSI vs ICSI (HABSelect)

factors.name: ICSI when sperm are normal (non-male-factor ICSI)
factors.headline: With normal sperm count and motility, ICSI did not beat conventional IVF in a 1064-couple Lancet RCT (live birth 35% vs 31%, NS; fertilisation failure 5% vs 6%), yet US registry data show two-thirds of non-male-factor cycles use it; ESHRE and ASRM advise against routine use.

dose.effective: Use conventional IVF when semen is normal; reserve ICSI for male factor, prior fertilisation failure, PGT cycles or very few eggs.
dose.studied_range: Sibling and randomised comparisons with WHO-normal semen.
dose.too_much: Extra cost and lab time; skips natural sperm selection at the egg's surface.
dose.timeframe: Fertilisation day.
dose.notes: Distinct from ICSI for genuine male factor, where it is the standard of care.

factors.mechanism: ICSI bypasses sperm binding and penetration; it rescues fertilisation when sperm cannot do this, but adds nothing when they can.
factors.interactions: Often combined with [sperm-selection-icsi-sperm]; high SDF is not by itself an indication for ICSI over IVF.
factors.caveats: Observational data even suggest slightly lower live birth with ICSI in non-male-factor cycles, but confounding is likely.
factors.debate: Some clinicians use ICSI routinely to avoid the small risk of total fertilisation failure; the Dang RCT found no difference in failure or live birth [fer-dang2021], and registry data found no benefit and slightly lower live birth (aRR 0.95) [fer-boulet2015]. ASRM and ESHRE advise against routine use [fer-asrm2020icsi, fer-eshre2023addons].

key_numbers.label: Live birth, ICSI vs conventional IVF (normal sperm)

factors.name: Iron overload and sperm
factors.headline: Pathological iron overload (thalassaemia, haemochromatosis) causes hypogonadism in about half of affected men and more sperm DNA damage; in ordinary men, higher seminal iron tracks with poorer motility, but there is no evidence that normal dietary iron harms sperm.

dose.effective: Men do not need iron supplements unless deficient; men with known iron overload need chelation or phlebotomy started early.
dose.studied_range: Median ferritin 2251 ug/L in thalassaemic men; observational seminal iron levels.
dose.too_much: Iron overload disorders: hypogonadism in ~47% of men, azoospermia in ~18% of those assessed.
dose.timeframe: Earlier chelation was associated with less sperm DNA damage.
dose.notes: Relevant mainly to men with thalassaemia, transfusion dependence or untreated haemochromatosis.

factors.mechanism: Iron deposits in the pituitary and testis; free iron catalyses Fenton chemistry and lipid peroxidation in polyunsaturated-rich sperm membranes; ferroptosis markers (low GPX4) appear in poor-motility sperm.
factors.interactions: Do not take iron-containing multivitamins without need [iron-excess]. Antioxidant supplements have not been tested in this group [male-antioxidant-combination].
factors.caveats: Evidence comes from tiny case series and case-control studies; seminal iron correlations are confounded by infection and leukocytes.
factors.debate: A systematic review of iron-overload disorders documents frequent hypogonadism and sperm abnormalities [nut-carlomagno2026], and a small study linked overload to sperm DNA damage [nut-perera2002]. Seminal iron correlates with poorer sperm quality [nut-ammar2019], but no study shows that dietary iron in non-overloaded men affects sperm; this extrapolation is unsupported.

Median ferritin, thalassaemic men with sperm DNA damage

factors.name: Flame retardants and semen quality
factors.headline: Higher dust TPHP went with 19% lower sperm concentration in 50 clinic men and PBDEs with lower motility in small studies, but the largest US fertility-clinic cohort found only weak, inconsistent links, and no study shows a sperm DNA-fragmentation effect.

dose.effective: Hand-washing before meals and wet cleaning lowered flame-retardant metabolites within a week; replace old foam furniture when practical.
dose.studied_range: Urinary OPFR metabolites in 220 EARTH men; dust TPHP and TDCPP in 50 men; serum PBDEs in 52-153 men.
dose.timeframe: Exposure during the roughly 74 days of spermatogenesis is what counts; OPFR body levels fall within days, PBDEs over years.
dose.notes: Strong co-exposure with phthalates and organophosphate pesticides; the one large Chinese "OPE" signal was driven by pesticide metabolites.

factors.mechanism: Thyroid and androgen disruption and Sertoli-cell oxidative stress in animals; in young men BDE-47 tracked motility but not sperm chromatin damage [eia-albert2018].
factors.interactions: See [flame-retardants]; overlaps with [plastics-chemicals] and [pesticides].
factors.caveats: Small samples, single urine samples, multiple metabolites and outcomes, and clinic populations. Paternal OPFRs were linked to fewer fertilized eggs and top-quality embryos in IVF, but not to live birth after adjusting for the female partner [eia-carignan2018].
factors.debate: Positive associations in small studies [eia-meeker2010, eia-abdelouahab2011, eia-yu2018] and a large Chinese clinic study [eia-li2023ope] versus weak and inconsistent results in 220 EARTH men [eia-ingle2018] and a 796-donor study where the mixture signal came from pesticide, not flame-retardant, metabolites [eia-tang2025]; borderline associations without DNA damage in healthy young men [eia-albert2018, eia-siddique2022].

key_numbers.label: Sperm concentration per IQR dust TPHP

factors.name: Occupational solvents and sperm (glycol ethers, paints, formaldehyde)
factors.headline: Men with high glycol ether or solvent exposure at work had 2-4 times the odds of low motile sperm count, and formaldehyde-exposed workers had lower motility; effects are sizeable for exposed workers but rest on case-referent and cross-sectional studies.

dose.effective: For about 3 months before trying to conceive, minimise exposure at work: local exhaust ventilation, respirator with organic-vapour cartridges, impermeable gloves, substitution of water-based products; ask for task reassignment if exposure is high.
dose.studied_range: Glycol ether exposure rated moderate/high by hygienists; shipyard painters 2-ethoxyethanol TWA mean 9.9 mg/m3; formaldehyde exposure index in Chinese factory workers.
dose.too_much: High glycol ether exposure: adjusted OR 2.25 for low motile count; high solvent exposure OR 2.9-3.8.
dose.timeframe: Sperm reflect roughly the last 74 days of exposure; the case-referent window was the 3 months before the clinic visit.
dose.notes: Hobby use (occasional painting, varnishing) in a ventilated space is far below the occupational exposures studied.

factors.mechanism: Alkoxyacetic acid metabolites of glycol ethers kill pachytene spermatocytes; solvents and formaldehyde raise lipid peroxidation, the main oxidative injury to sperm membranes.
factors.interactions: See [occupational-solvents]. Adds to heat ([everyday-scrotal-heat]) and smoking, which travel with manual work.
factors.caveats: Job-based exposure assessment; confounding by heat, smoking and alcohol (adjustment reduced the glycol ether OR from 2.54 to 2.25). The most toxic glycol ethers have been restricted.
factors.debate: Two independent case-referent series (Canada, UK) found dose-related associations [eia-cherry2001, eia-cherry2008] and painters had more oligospermia [eia-welch1988], but in the Canadian replication series moderate exposure showed no effect (OR 1.01) [eia-cherry2001], and the time-to-pregnancy literature for solvents is equivocal [eia-snijder2012]. Formaldehyde-motility findings come from two Chinese occupational studies with exposure indices [eia-wang2015fa, eia-lv2022] and await replication.

factors.name: Parabens and sperm
factors.headline: Studies of urinary parabens and semen disagree: the Boston clinic study (190 men) and a Japanese study found no link with semen quality, while a 795-man Chinese study and smaller Polish and Chinese studies reported lower count or motility or more DNA damage; no study shows that cutting parabens improves sperm.

dose.effective: Use paraben-free leave-on products, especially sunscreen and body lotion (their use within 6 h raised men's urinary parabens 66-156% and 79-147%). For semen collected for testing, IUI or IVF, avoid paraben-preserved lubricants ([lubricants-sperm]).
dose.studied_range: Single or duplicate spot urines in men from fertility clinics and preconception cohorts (n = 42-795).
dose.too_much: No human threshold. In vitro, methylparaben at concentrations used in clinical products and lubricants cut motility and raised ROS and oxidative DNA adducts.
dose.timeframe: Exposure clears within days; any effect on sperm would need about one spermatogenic cycle (roughly 2-3 months) to show.
dose.notes: Butylparaben, the most potent and least common paraben, carries most of the positive findings.

factors.mechanism: Parabens raise mitochondrial ROS and oxidative DNA adducts in human sperm in vitro, more with longer chains [epc-samarasinghe2018]; they are weakly estrogenic and anti-androgenic.
factors.interactions: Co-exposure with phthalates and BPA ([plastics-chemicals]); see [parabens] for sources and [lubricants-sperm].
factors.caveats: All human studies are cross-sectional or clinic-based, many on single urines, with mixtures of correlated chemicals and many semen endpoints tested (multiple-testing risk). Positive findings cluster in mixture models and for butylparaben, which is detected in only a minority of samples.
factors.debate: Null: no association with semen quality in 190 Boston men (butylparaben only with DNA damage) [epc-meeker2011], 42 Japanese men [epc-nishihama2017], or Spanish young men's DNA fragmentation [epc-kiwitt2024]; paternal parabens were not linked to IVF fertilization or live birth [epc-dodge2015]. Positive: lower motility and more abnormal forms and DNA stainability in 315 Polish men [epc-jurewicz2017], lower count and motility with a paraben mixture in 795 Chinese men [epc-shen2023], and butylparaben with comet-assay DNA damage [epc-li2026]. No meta-analysis exists.

key_numbers.label: Largest semen study (paraben mixture, lower count/motility)
Rise in men's urinary parabens with sunscreen use

factors.name: Triclosan and sperm
factors.headline: A 2024 meta-analysis of 5 small case-control and cross-sectional studies linked triclosan to lower sperm concentration and motility (high heterogeneity); the larger Boston study found only about 1 percentage point fewer normal-shaped sperm without dose-response, and a 443-couple Shanghai cohort linked higher male triclosan to 23% lower fecundability.

dose.effective: Use plain soap and triclosan-free toothpaste, deodorant and cosmetics; most US consumer washes have been triclosan-free since 2017.
dose.studied_range: Urinary or seminal-plasma triclosan in 262-471 men; one preconception cohort of 443 couples.
dose.too_much: No human threshold.
dose.timeframe: Triclosan clears in about 1-4 days; sperm effects, if any, would take a spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: Exposure in the US has fallen since the FDA rule, so older studies reflect higher exposure.

factors.mechanism: Endocrine disruption (androgen and thyroid pathways) and oxidative stress in animal and in vitro testis models.
factors.interactions: See [triclosan-triclocarban] for sources; co-exposure with [parabens].
factors.caveats: Small, mainly clinic-based, cross-sectional studies with single urines; pooled estimates are dominated by heterogeneity.
factors.debate: Positive: meta-analysis SMD -0.42 for concentration and -1.30 for motility [epc-adegbola2024]; modest motility links in 471 men [epc-zhu2016]; lower fecundability with male triclosan [epc-zhu2022]. Weak or null: limited (none or modest) effects in 406 men [epc-yuan2022]; only slightly lower morphology without dose-response in 262 Boston men [epc-nassan2019]; a systematic review found little to no indication that triclosan affects time to pregnancy [epc-hipwell2019].

factors.name: Sunscreen UV filters and sperm
factors.headline: Mostly null: in the US LIFE study men's urinary BP-2 (not the main sunscreen filter BP-3) went with 31% lower couple fecundability and some poorer semen measures, while Spanish and Danish studies found no semen links overall; several filters trigger sperm calcium signalling in a dish.

dose.effective: Keep using sunscreen; if trying to conceive, prefer mineral (zinc oxide or titanium dioxide) sunscreen and protective clothing to reduce absorbed filters.
dose.studied_range: Urinary benzophenones in 413-501 men (LIFE), young men in Spain and Denmark.
dose.too_much: No human threshold. In vitro calcium effects began at nanomolar to micromolar concentrations for some filters.
dose.timeframe: BP-3 is excreted over about 5 days after use; sperm effects, if any, would take a spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: The filters most linked to semen findings (BP-2, BP-8, 4-hydroxybenzophenone) are not the main ones in modern sunscreens.

factors.mechanism: Thirteen of 29 UV filters induced calcium influx in human sperm, nine via CatSper, mimicking progesterone and potentially disturbing timing of hyperactivation and the acrosome reaction [epc-rehfeld2016]; benzophenones are weakly estrogenic and anti-androgenic.
factors.interactions: Weigh against the [sunscreen] benefit; see [uv-filters].
factors.caveats: Many semen endpoints and several filters were tested per study, so isolated hits are expected by chance. Associations appeared only in men with skin-barrier (filaggrin) mutations in one study [epc-joensen2018].
factors.debate: Positive: male BP-2 and 4OH-BP with lower fecundability [epc-buck2014]; BP-2 and BP-8 with a few of 35 semen endpoints [epc-buck2015]; a 2025 review sees a benzophenone-sperm signal [epc-jaskulak2025]. Null or opposite: no semen associations for any BP filter in Spanish young men, only small FSH shifts [epc-adoamnei2018]; 4OH-BP with slightly lower DNA fragmentation [epc-kiwitt2024]; associations limited to filaggrin-mutation carriers [epc-joensen2018]. A systematic review called the male benzophenone-TTP link preliminary [epc-hipwell2019].

key_numbers.label: UV filters inducing sperm calcium signals in vitro

factors.name: Phthalates and sperm
factors.headline: Men with higher urinary DBP and BBzP metabolites (MBP, MBzP) have roughly twice the odds of low sperm concentration in pooled data, and DEP and DEHP metabolites tracked 14-18% more Comet sperm DNA damage in one Boston clinic, but nearly all of it comes from single spot urines in fertility-clinic men, motility and morphology links are null in meta-analysis, and no trial shows that lowering exposure improves semen.

dose.effective: Same steps as [phthalates]: fresh rather than fast or ultra-processed food, glass or steel for hot food, fragrance-free toiletries and aftershave, and phthalate-free formulations of long-term enteric-coated medicines (with a pharmacist). Start about 3 months before trying to conceive.
dose.studied_range: General-population and fertility-clinic urinary levels; single spot urine in most studies, repeated samples in a 1,034-man Chinese cohort.
dose.too_much: No semen threshold established. EFSA group TDI 50 ug/kg/day (DEHP equivalents) is set on fetal testosterone, not adult sperm.
dose.timeframe: Urine falls within 1-3 days; any change in sperm would need roughly one spermatogenic cycle (about 64 days plus epididymal transit, so about 3 months).
dose.notes: No intervention study has measured semen or sperm DNA fragmentation.

factors.mechanism: Phthalate monoesters are Sertoli- and Leydig-cell toxicants in rodents and lower testosterone; in men from subfertile couples, every urinary phthalate metabolite tracked oxidative-stress markers (8-OHdG, 8-isoPGF2a, HNE-MA), and 8-isoPGF2a suggestively mediated about 12% of the MBP-sperm concentration association. Comet-assay damage is consistent with oxidative DNA breaks but was not measured alongside oxidative markers.
factors.interactions: Shares sources with [bisphenols-sperm] and [microplastics-sperm]; men with higher exposure also tend to eat more processed food, so [profertility-diet] confounds. Paternal DEHP was also linked to lower IVF live birth in couples (see [phthalates-egg]).
factors.caveats: Cross-sectional fertility-clinic samples (selection into IVF clinics), one urine per man for metabolites with ICC 0.1-0.6, many metabolite-by-endpoint tests, and confounding by diet and BMI. The MEHP-DNA-damage finding appeared only after statistically adjusting for its own oxidative metabolite MEHHP, a modelling choice. Sperm DNA damage was measured with the neutral Comet assay, not the clinical SCSA/TUNEL tests.
factors.debate: For: an EPA systematic review rated evidence 'robust' for DEHP and DBP and male reproductive outcomes (AGD, semen, testosterone) [ept-radke2018]; clinic studies found dose-response links of MBP with low concentration [ept-hauser2006] and of MEP and MEHP with Comet DNA damage [ept-duty2003, ept-hauser2007]; a 2026 systematic review graded certainty low to moderate [ept-dhar2026]; oxidative stress may partly mediate [ept-liu2019]. Against or narrower: a meta-analysis found only MBP, MBzP and semen DEHP associated with concentration and nothing for motility or morphology [ept-wangh2023]; in 420 EARTH men a mixture analysis of 24 chemicals found the consistent signals were mercury and triclosan, not phthalates [ept-genardwalton2025]. Paternal exposure and couple outcomes: a few paternal metabolites predicted lower implantation and live birth but most did not [ept-dodge2015]; a paternal DEHP factor predicted IVF failure (HR 1.41) [ept-minguezalarcon2021].

factors.name: Bisphenols (BPA, BPS) and sperm
factors.headline: Pooled studies find at most a slight link between urinary BPA and lower sperm concentration and count, and a motility link vanished after publication-bias correction; a 190-man clinic study tied BPA to 10% more Comet DNA damage, but a 418-man population cohort found higher BPA with slightly less DNA fragmentation, so the DNA-damage claim is unconfirmed.

dose.effective: Same steps as [bisphenols]: fewer canned foods and drinks, no old polycarbonate bottles, decline or briefly handle receipts (not after hand sanitizer), fresh food. Start about 3 months before trying to conceive.
dose.studied_range: Urinary BPA medians about 0.5-1.9 ug/L in general-population and clinic studies; much higher in Chinese BPA factory workers.
dose.too_much: No semen threshold established. Germany's BfR based its proposed BPA TDI (1,000-fold above EFSA's 0.2 ng/kg/day) on sperm-count declines after adult exposure.
dose.timeframe: Urinary BPA turns over within a day; any sperm effect would need about one spermatogenic cycle (roughly 3 months).
dose.notes: Clear harm is seen mainly at occupational exposures; at everyday levels results are inconsistent.

factors.mechanism: Estrogenic and anti-androgenic activity (higher SHBG and estradiol, lower bioactive androgens in pooled data), with oxidative stress proposed but not measured in the semen studies cited here.
factors.interactions: Co-exposed with [phthalates-sperm]; BPS associations were concentrated in overweight men ([excess-adiposity]).
factors.caveats: Single spot urines for a chemical with a 6-hour half-life (ICC about 0.1-0.2), clinic populations, many endpoints, and possible publication bias.
factors.debate: For: men with workplace exposure had 3-4 times the risk of low concentration and count, persisting at environmental levels [ept-li2011]; in a clinic, an IQR rise in BPA went with 23% lower concentration and 10% more Comet DNA damage [ept-meeker2010]; a 2024 meta-analysis found small falls in concentration and count [ept-lu2024]; detectable BPS went with lower concentration, mainly in overweight men [ept-ghayda2019]. Against: a meta-analysis of 2,399 men found only a weak motility link that disappeared after publication-bias correction and called it clinically negligible [ept-castellini2022]; in the population-based LIFE study the only finding among 35 semen measures was less DNA fragmentation with higher BPA [ept-goldstone2015]; in 158 young Spanish men there was no overall link with DNA fragmentation [ept-kiwittcardenas2021]. Regulators split on whether adult sperm effects should set the safe dose [ept-kortenkamp2024].

factors.name: Glyphosate and sperm
factors.headline: Glyphosate has been measured in seminal plasma at about four times blood levels, where it tracked 8-OHdG and MDA in 128 infertile French men, but no study links typical dietary glyphosate to semen quality, and in vitro it cut motility only at concentrations far above real exposure.

dose.effective: No sperm-specific intervention has been tested. Practical steps are the general ones in [glyphosate]: gloves and long sleeves when spraying, and organic grains and legumes if you want to cut dietary intake.
dose.studied_range: Seminal plasma glyphosate in infertile men (French cohort); 0.36 mg/L in vitro.
dose.too_much: Not defined for sperm. Occupational spraying without protection gives the highest exposure.
dose.timeframe: Glyphosate clears from urine within days, but any effect on sperm would take at least one round of spermatogenesis (about 64 days, plus epididymal transit) to appear or reverse [efw-heller1963].
dose.notes: Most animal reproductive studies use formulations with surfactants, which are more toxic than glyphosate itself.

factors.mechanism: In vitro and in animals, glyphosate-based herbicides damage sperm membranes (largely via surfactants), lower testosterone production in Leydig cells and raise testicular ROS. In men, seminal glyphosate tracked seminal 8-OHdG and men with detectable glyphosate had higher total oxidant status and MDA [efw-vasseur2024].
factors.interactions: General exposure data and reduction steps: [glyphosate]. Often co-occurs with other pesticides in farm work ([pesticides], [organophosphates]).
factors.caveats: One cross-sectional study of infertile men without a fertile comparison group or adjustment for other pesticides; ELISA-based oxidative markers. The in vitro study used 0.36 mg/L, far above environmental levels, and found no DNA-fragmentation effect [efw-anifandis2018].
factors.debate: Pro-harm: glyphosate concentrates in seminal plasma and tracks oxidative DNA damage there [efw-vasseur2024]; NHANES urinary glyphosate was cross-sectionally associated with lower sex steroids and AMH [efw-wu2025]. Against: in vitro, glyphosate lowered motility only at high concentrations and did not raise DNA fragmentation [efw-anifandis2018]; EFSA and ECHA concluded glyphosate is not a reproductive toxicant [efw-efsa2023].

factors.name: Pyrethroid insecticides and sperm
factors.headline: Cross-sectional clinic studies link urinary pyrethroid metabolites to lower sperm concentration and more sperm DNA damage, but meta-analyses of 12 cross-sectional studies are inconsistent (lower motility overall; concentration lower in Poland but higher in the US).

dose.effective: No intervention tested on sperm. Use the exposure steps in [pyrethroids]: peel or cook produce, choose organic for high-residue items, and limit indoor insecticide, flea-treatment and treated-clothing use.
dose.studied_range: Urinary 3-PBA and DCCA metabolites in clinic men (n = 207-240 per study).
dose.too_much: Not defined.
dose.timeframe: Metabolites clear within a day; any sperm effect would follow the ~64-day course of spermatogenesis [efw-heller1963].
dose.notes: Studies used a single urine sample against a semen sample that reflects about 3 months of exposure.

factors.mechanism: Pyrethroids show anti-androgenic and oxidative effects in rodent testes. In men, 3-PBA tracked sperm DNA fragmentation (beta 0.27) [efw-ji2011] and comet-assay DNA damage [efw-meeker2008].
factors.interactions: General exposure: [pyrethroids]. Often studied together with [organophosphates]; occupational data in [pesticides].
factors.caveats: All studies are cross-sectional with one urine sample and poor exposure reliability [efw-lin2021]; small clinic samples; publication bias untested.
factors.debate: Positive studies found lower concentration and more sperm DNA damage [efw-meeker2008, efw-ji2011]. Meta-analyses disagree: one found pyrethroids linked only to fewer normal-morphology sperm [efw-giulioni2021], another to lower motility with region-dependent, sometimes opposite, effects on concentration [efw-akhigbe2024].

factors.name: Chlorination by-products and sperm
factors.headline: Chinese studies measuring blood trihalomethanes found lower sperm count and concentration (including repeated-measure data in 1,199 men), but the largest study using tap-water levels (642 cases, 926 referents in England and Wales) found no link (OR 1.01 per 10 ug/L).

dose.effective: No sperm-specific intervention tested. If your water is high in THMs, a carbon-filter pitcher or under-sink filter for drinking and shorter, ventilated showers lower exposure ([disinfection-byproducts]).
dose.studied_range: Blood THMs in Chinese men; tap-water THM 0-100 ug/L in UK and US studies.
dose.too_much: Not defined; associations appeared within regulatory ranges.
dose.timeframe: Blood THMs fall within hours; sperm effects would take at least ~64 days (one round of spermatogenesis) to change [efw-heller1963].
dose.notes: Blood THM reflects only the last few hours of showering and drinking.

factors.mechanism: Brominated THMs and haloacetic acids produce oxidative stress and lower testosterone in animal studies; GST genotypes modify metabolism.
factors.interactions: General exposure and reduction: [disinfection-byproducts].
factors.caveats: Positive studies come largely from one Wuhan research group; blood THM is a snapshot; many THM species and semen endpoints were tested.
factors.debate: Harm: blood THMs tracked lower sperm count in 1,199 donors [efw-chen2020] and in other Wuhan samples [efw-zeng2014, efw-zeng2013]; an early US study found fewer normal-morphology sperm with high ingestion [efw-fenster2003]. No harm: the England and Wales case-referent study found none [efw-iszatt2013].

mechanisms.name: Why sperm are uniquely vulnerable
mechanisms.description: Sperm membranes are rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids such as DHA, which are easily peroxidised. During maturation sperm shed almost all cytoplasm, so they carry very little superoxide dismutase, catalase or glutathione peroxidase and rely on seminal plasma for protection. They are transcriptionally silent and have only the first enzyme of base excision repair (OGG1), so oxidised bases are excised but the gaps cannot be filled.

mechanisms.name: Aitken's two-step hypothesis of sperm DNA damage
mechanisms.description: Step 1: defective spermiogenesis leaves sperm with poor histone-to-protamine replacement, retained cytoplasm and loose chromatin. Step 2: oxidative stress (from the sperm's own mitochondria, from leukocytes, or from heat and toxicants) attacks this vulnerable DNA, forming 8-OHdG; OGG1 excises the lesion, leaving abasic sites that break into the strand breaks measured as SDF.

mechanisms.name: Mitochondrial ROS and apoptosis in sperm
mechanisms.description: Stressed or defective sperm leak electrons at mitochondrial complex I, producing superoxide and hydrogen peroxide; this triggers a truncated apoptotic cascade. Hydrogen peroxide from the midpiece crosses into the nucleus and damages DNA, while lipid peroxidation products (e.g. 4-hydroxynonenal) further poison mitochondria in a self-propagating loop.

mechanisms.name: Leukocyte NADPH oxidase
mechanisms.description: Activated neutrophils and macrophages in semen generate superoxide via NOX2 at far higher rates than sperm; infection and inflammation therefore produce oxidative bursts that overwhelm seminal antioxidants.

mechanisms.name: Oocyte repair of paternal DNA damage
mechanisms.description: After fertilisation the oocyte must complete base excision repair of the sperm's oxidised DNA before the first S-phase; unrepaired or misrepaired lesions become mutations present in every cell of the embryo. This repair capacity is limited and appears to fall with maternal age, which is why high SDF hurts ICSI outcomes mostly in women over 40.

mechanisms.name: Scrotal thermoregulation
mechanisms.description: Spermatogenesis needs a testicular temperature about 2-4 C below core. Heat disrupts protamination and mitochondrial function in developing germ cells and induces apoptosis, effects that appear 2-3 months later and reverse within about 3-6 months of removing the heat.

mechanisms.name: Reductive stress and chromatin compaction
mechanisms.description: Some ROS are needed: protamine disulphide bridges form oxidatively during epididymal transit, and capacitation needs a controlled oxidative burst. Large antioxidant doses can reduce these bonds and impair compaction, a proposed reason why antioxidant trials are inconsistent.

mechanisms.name: Spermatogenesis timeline
mechanisms.description: The textbook duration of spermatogenesis is about 74 days, based on 1960s labelling studies. Direct isotope labelling found new sperm first reaching the ejaculate about 64 days (range 42-76) after they started forming, including epididymal transit. Changes made today therefore start to show in about 2 months and are fully reflected after about 3 months.

mechanisms.name: What high sperm DNA fragmentation does clinically
mechanisms.description: High SDF is associated with longer time to natural pregnancy (fecundability falls as SCSA abnormal sperm rise, becoming small above 30-40%), about double the miscarriage risk (RR 2.16), higher SDF in partners of women with recurrent pregnancy loss (+11.9 points), and lower clinical pregnancy and live birth after IVF and, to a lesser extent, ICSI. Double-strand breaks may matter most for miscarriage. Associations are consistent but heterogeneous, and SDF predicts outcomes imperfectly.

mechanisms.name: Sperm DNA fragmentation and oxidative stress tests
mechanisms.description: SCSA (flow cytometry after acid denaturation; DFI, classic cut-off 25-30%), TUNEL (labels strand-break ends; flow cut-off about 17-20%), SCD/Halo (halo size after protein removal; ~20-30%) and Comet (single-cell electrophoresis; alkaline detects single- and double-strand breaks, neutral mainly double-strand). Expert guidelines use thresholds near 20% (about 26% for alkaline Comet). ASRM (2013) and AUA/ASRM (2020/2024) do not recommend SDF in the initial work-up but do for recurrent pregnancy loss; EAU recommends it for recurrent pregnancy loss, ART failure and unexplained infertility. MiOXSYS ORP is quick but its normalisation to sperm concentration makes it highly sensitive and poorly specific (40.6%), and EAU advises against routine ROS testing.
